opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the phrase "letting loose" can sound a bit more dramatic than what we actually mean in practice.

When I talk about open-endedness, the core idea is that we want systems that keep generating artifacts that are both novel and learnable for an observer. Things that are surprising but that you can still make sense of and learn from. And if you take that seriously, you do need to give agents some degree of autonomy. You can't hand-specify every task, because the whole point is that the system discovers things you didn't anticipate. If I could write down all the interesting problems in advance, I wouldn't need an open-ended system in the first place.

But autonomy isn't binary. There's a spectrum. On one end you have very constrained settings: an agent exploring procedurally generated environments, or proposing new tasks for itself in a simulator, where the blast radius is essentially zero. That's where a lot of our research has lived, and it's a fantastic sandbox for understanding the dynamics of self-improvement and curriculum generation. On the other end you have agents acting in the real world, running code, interacting with the web, maybe running experiments. That's a very different situation, and the level of autonomy you're comfortable granting should scale with how reversible and how observable those actions are.

What I find interesting is that open-endedness itself is defined relative to an observer. Novelty and learnability are judged by someone, and in many settings that someone is us, humans. So in a sense humans are baked into the loop by definition. The system is supposed to produce things we find interesting and can learn from, not wander off into some region that's meaningless or incomprehensible to us. I think that's a useful framing for safety too: we want open-ended systems whose discoveries stay legible to humans, where we can follow along, verify, and steer.

So my view is roughly this. Autonomous exploration is necessary if we want AI to go beyond the data we've already given it, to actually generate new knowledge. But we should be thoughtful about where we let that autonomy play out. Push hard on it in safe, sandboxed domains, build good tools for oversight and interpretability, and expand the scope gradually as we earn confidence. It's less about letting agents loose and more about designing the environments and feedback loops so that exploration is productive and stays aligned with what we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response connects safety to keeping discoveries legible to humans so they can follow, verify, and steer the agents.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says autonomy is a spectrum, from constrained simulated settings to agents acting in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should be careful with the phrase "letting loose," because I think it conjures up images of agents running around the internet doing whatever they want, and that's not really what I mean. What I'm talking about is open-ended exploration inside environments that we design and control. So think of something like NetHack, or the kinds of procedurally generated worlds we've been building with things like MiniHack or XLand. In those settings, "autonomy" means the agent gets to decide what to try next, what sub-goals to set for itself, what's interesting, rather than us hand-specifying a curriculum. And that's really important, because I think the big lesson from the last decade is that humans are actually quite bad at knowing what the right next stepping stone is for a learning system. Open-endedness is about letting the system, or the system together with an environment generator, discover those stepping stones itself.

Now, the obvious question is, what happens when that kind of autonomy leaves the sandbox? And I think there are two things to say. The first is that the capability to explore and the permission to act in the world are separable, and we should keep them separate for as long as we need to. You can have an agent that's extremely good at generating and solving its own problems in simulation, and still have a very narrow interface to anything with real consequences. The second is that, somewhat counterintuitively, I think open-endedness research is one of the better tools we have for understanding what these systems actually do when you give them room. If you only ever evaluate on a fixed benchmark, you never see the weird, out-of-distribution behaviour until it shows up in deployment. Whereas if your whole research program is "generate situations nobody anticipated and see how the agent copes," you're building the muscle for exactly the kind of robustness and oversight you want before you give the system more rope. So I'd put it this way: I'm quite enthusiastic about agents being autonomous in the sense of being self-directed learners, and quite conservative about them being autonomous in the sense of unsupervised actors. The research is about the first one, and I think doing it well is actually how you earn the right to think carefully about the second.

r001.rationale: It discusses controlled environments, separating capability from permission, and building oversight, but does not identify AI safety as a reason humans should provide direction to agents.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes self-directed learning within designed environments from unsupervised action in the real world, framing autonomy as different degrees or forms rather than an all-or-nothing choice.

astra-6.text:
I think there are different levels of autonomy here. You can give an agent a lot of freedom to explore within an environment without giving it unrestricted access to the world. Those are quite different things.

For me, the interesting question is whether an agent can discover useful things without us having to specify every task in advance. Can it set itself challenges, learn from trying to solve them, and build skills that become useful later? If we prescribe everything it should do, we also limit what it can discover.

But that freedom needs a boundary. What can the agent actually affect? What feedback does it get? Can we stop it or reset the environment? You might allow very open-ended exploration in a simulation while being much more careful about actions that have consequences outside it. So I’d think of “letting loose” as giving the agent room to discover within a deliberately chosen setting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses setting boundaries and limiting consequences, but does not clearly identify AI safety as a reason for humans to provide agents with direction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes different levels of autonomy, contrasting freedom to explore within an environment with unrestricted access to the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think autonomy is a spectrum. You can give an agent freedom to explore within an environment without giving it unrestricted access to the world. And that distinction is quite important. In a simulated environment, for example, an agent can try things, fail, and discover behaviors that we wouldn’t have thought to specify ourselves, while we still control the boundaries of what it can do.

The exciting question for me is how you get agents to go beyond simply solving the task you’ve given them—to explore, develop new skills, and potentially discover problems worth solving. But that doesn’t mean taking humans out of the picture. We’re still designing the environment, the learning process, and the constraints. “Letting loose” means allowing room for discovery within those boundaries.

r001.rationale: The response says humans design the environment and constraints, but does not identify AI safety as a reason for providing that direction.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly describes autonomy as a spectrum and frames exploration as freedom within boundaries.
